title: The jewel of peace
hook: Sukhmani means the jewel of peace; many read it daily or in groups when life is hard
carry: resting in the middle of it

segments.voice: Yesterday, sukhasan, and your line was sleep in praise. Were the last words you heard last night good ones? Today a new bani begins, and it will stay with us a while. Day four hundred thirty-six.

A family has just moved into a new house. Boxes still line the hall, but before the furniture is in place, a few relatives sit together on the floor, each holding a small book, reading aloud in a low, steady rhythm. The same scene can turn up the night before an exam, in the month after a funeral, in a week of bad news. Sometimes it's a circle of neighbors who meet every week to do just this. What they're reading is Sukhmani Sahib, a bani Sikh families turn to when life is hard, and when it's new.
screen: `A NEW HOUSE, BOXES IN THE HALL.` → `PEOPLE READING ALOUD TOGETHER.` → `THE BANI THEY REACH FOR: SUKHMANI.`

segments.voice: Sukhmani. Sukh means peace, comfort, ease, the opposite of dukh, pain. Mani means a jewel; some also hear man, the mind, in it. So Sukhmani is the jewel of peace, or the peace of the mind. Sahib is added out of respect. It was composed by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, the same Guru who wrote Sohila's last hymn and compiled the scripture. Tradition says he wrote it at a quiet pool near Amritsar called Ramsar, around the time the scripture was being gathered. It sits in Raag Gauri, beginning on Ang 262 of the Guru Granth Sahib. And it's long. Twenty-four sections, each one opening with a short salok and followed by eight stanzas. Near the beginning, Guru Arjan gives the whole bani its own name. In paraphrase: Sukhmani, the jewel of peace, is the nectar of God's Name; it rests in the minds of the devoted. Notice what that line says peace is. Not a feeling you chase. Not a place you get to after the problems are solved. Peace is the Name, remembering God, and it rests in a mind the way a jewel rests in a box. That's why families open it when life is hard. The hospital room doesn't change. The test is still tomorrow. But the Sikh hope is that something steady can rest in the middle of it. Over the next hundred days, we'll walk through Sukhmani section by section.
screen: `SUKH: PEACE. MANI: A JEWEL.` · `GURU ARJAN, AT RAMSAR.` · `TWENTY-FOUR SECTIONS, EIGHT STANZAS EACH.` · `PEACE RESTS IN A MIND.` · then, large: `THE JEWEL OF PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to the opening. If you can, find a recording of Sukhmani Sahib and play the first minute or two, just the sound, even if you don't follow the words. If you can't right now, sit quietly and picture one of those living rooms: people side by side, books open, voices low. Let the steadiness of it reach you. Then breathe slowly and notice one place in your body that's tight, and let it soften. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. The bell holds the time.
Sukhmani. The jewel of peace: Guru Arjan's long bani of twenty-four sections, read daily by some Sikhs and in groups when life is hard.
Your line: resting in the middle of it. Today, when something hard comes up, imagine a small jewel resting in the middle of it, and come back to that picture once. Day four hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Some Sikhs read Sukhmani Sahib daily, often in the morning, and families and sangats gather to read it together in times of illness, grief, celebration and new beginnings, such as moving into a new home.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Sukhmani, the jewel of peace; Guru Arjan's bani in Raag Gauri.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sukhmani is a calming prayer.
what it means: the jewel of peace, a long bani teaching that peace is the nectar of God's Name resting in the mind.
what a scholar hears: Guru Arjan's Gauri Sukhmani (Ang 262–296) has 24 ashtpadis, each preceded by a salok; tradition places its composition at Ramsar, Amritsar.
recall: the wedding date, fixed in advance

sources.ref: Gauri Sukhmani M5, Ang 262 (opening and rahau)

notes: Mani glossed as jewel, with the alternative reading man (mind); confirm both are standard.
Composition at Ramsar near Amritsar, around the time the Adi Granth was being compiled (c. 1602–1604): told as tradition; confirm.
Ang 262 as the start of Sukhmani (it runs to about Ang 296): confirm.
Rahau paraphrased ('Sukhmani, the jewel of peace, is the nectar of God's Name; it rests in the minds of the devoted'); confirm.
Weekly Sukhmani Sahib groups of women: widely observed; phrased generally. Confirm.
'Over the next hundred days': Block G runs days 436–535 per the outline.
